conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for taking this time to talk with me.  
I’m Dr. Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. For every new mom, we routinely use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to see how you’ve really been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within your care team. My goal is to make sure you feel safe and supported while we do this.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  
To start: over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Yeah… I can still laugh sometimes. Like, if my partner makes a joke or I see something silly on my phone, I’ll chuckle. It just doesn’t come as easily as it used to—feels like I have to remind myself to enjoy it, you know.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh sometimes. Like, if my partner makes a joke or I see something silly on my phone, I’ll chuckle. It just doesn’t come as easily as it used to—feels like I have to remind myself to enjoy it, you know.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some stuff—like my mom coming over or the baby giving me one of those big gummy smiles—but the excitement is kind of muted. Before I’d be counting the minutes; now it’s more “oh, that’ll be nice,” and then I worry I won’t even feel it when it happens.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. The other night the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I should’ve been able to calm her down faster. I know, logically, babies just cry, but I still felt like I must’ve missed something or wasn’t doing enough.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, even though she’s right there in my arms. Nothing triggered it—no story on the news or anything—just this quick wave of worry that I have to talk myself down from. It passes, but it keeps popping up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had any real panic, but once or twice I’ve felt this sudden rush of “what if I can’t handle this?”—heart beats a little faster, I get kind of shaky, and then it fades. Nothing’s actually wrong in the moment; it just hits out of nowhere and leaves me a bit rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I manage fine, but a couple of times this week it felt like the to-do list just kept growing—laundry, bottles, texts I haven’t answered—and I got that tight-chest feeling. I didn’t shut down or anything; I just had to stop, take a breath, and tackle one thing at a time until the pressure eased.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it isn’t that bad. I fall asleep okay once the baby settles, maybe twenty minutes of tossing if I’m stewing over the day, but I still get a decent stretch. I’m tired, but the sadness isn’t keeping me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel kind of down some days. Not the whole day, but it’s like this cloud that drifts in—especially in the late afternoon when everything’s been go-go-go with the baby. I’ll just feel heavy and teary for a bit, then it lifts. It’s happened maybe three or four times this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times—once when she wouldn’t nap and I felt like I was failing, and another night when I dropped a whole bottle of pumped milk. It was more frustration than sobbing, but yeah, the tears came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds as though you're working very hard to keep everything afloat while carrying a quiet heaviness that drifts in most afternoons. You can still laugh and anticipate small joys, yet the sparkle feels dimmer and worries pop up uninvited-especially about your baby's wellbeing-leaving you rattled and teary. These waves of self-blame, occasional panic-like surges, and several crying spells over the past week tell me your emotional load is heavier than it should be, even though you continue to cope and you consistently reject any thought of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>She still anticipates events but reports noticeably diminished excitement and worries the feeling won't arrive, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame ('I catch myself doing that') with a specific recent example, matching 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, unprovoked worry episodes that she must actively talk herself down from, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, noticeable sadness several times this week—fits "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 13 falls within the 12-13 range indicating high likelihood of <med>postpartum depression</med>. The patient describes core symptoms aligned with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartonset</med>: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>muted excitement</sym>), inappropriate guilt (<sym>self-blame for infant fussing</sym>), recurrent sadness, and anxiety without external triggers. She meets "more days than not" frequency for several items and shows functional impact (need to pace tasks). <quote>I felt like I was failing</quote> supports negative self-concept, while <quote>quick wave of worry that I have to talk myself down from</quote> indicates associated anxiety. Safety screening was negative. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange prompt appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full diagnostic evaluation
2. Continue weekly supportive check-ins with your partner or family; share Edinburgh score so they understand you need extra help
3. Build 15-20 min daily "you-time" for rest or gentle exercise while a trusted adult minds baby; adequate rest improves mood
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when <sym>anxiety</sym> surges-inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s-to calm autonomic arousal
5. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks; if score remains ≥12 or functioning declines, pursue therapy or medication discussion sooner
6. If any thought of self-harm ever develops, call your provider, a crisis line, or 911 immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report, 2–3 wks postpartum.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Diminished enjoyment/pleasure (Q1, Q2) — “muted” excitement, effort to laugh  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (Q3) — attributes infant fussing to personal failure  
- Unprovoked anxiety/worry (Q4) — sudden concerns about infant breathing  
- Mild panicky surges (Q5) — episodic “what-if-I-can’t-handle-this,” autonomic arousal  
- Intermittent sadness/tearfulness (Q8, Q9) — late-afternoon “cloud,” crying when stressed  
- Feeling overwhelmed (Q6) — chest tightness when tasks accumulate, improved with pacing

Symptoms denied  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood (Q7)  
- Self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present several days/week; no functional shutdown; no safety concerns at this time.

Risk factors noted  
- > 2 wk of anhedonia, guilt, crying spells  
- Anxious ruminations & brief panic-like episodes  
- No suicidal thoughts; protective factor: responsive support system (partner, mother)

Screening impression  
Meets partial criteria for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; scores suggest above-threshold distress warranting further evaluation (diagnostic interview, PHQ-9/EPDS, differential for GAD, adjustment disorder). Continue routine pediatric visits; consider referral to perinatal mental health specialist for assessment and psychoeducation.
